chunks: "The ones I'd quote are: 50 ohms single-ended is the default for RF and for most digital PCB traces, and it's what scopes, cables and test gear are built around.
75 ohms is video and cable TV. For differential pairs, 100 ohms is the most common: Ethernet, PCIe, SATA, HDMI, DisplayPort, LVDS. USB is the exception at 90 ohms.
And 120 ohms is for CAN and RS-485 buses, because that's the characteristic impedance of the twisted pair cable.
DDR memory has its own single-ended values, roughly 40 to 60 ohms depending on the generation and the vendor's layout guide. Why 50? In coax there's a trade-off.
For a given outer diameter, attenuation is lowest around 77 ohms and power handling is highest around 30 ohms, and 50 is a good compromise.
On a PCB, 50 ohms is also convenient: it gives a trace width that's easy to fabricate and a line that a typical CMOS driver can handle.
On a board, I don't pick the number, the interface does.
I pick the stackup and width to hit it, usually with the fab's field solver, and the tolerance is about plus or minus 10 percent.
And remember that the differential impedance isn't just twice 50 when the pair is coupled."
